description: I int in website and design engineering
summary:
Field Shift helps farmers decide which crop to plant next. Rotation protects soil, saves water and reduces risk, but the right choice depends on soil moisture, rainfall, temperature, terrain, soil quality and market demand. That data is scattered across dozens of portals, so many decisions rely on habit, not evidence.
Field Shift combines NASA, USDA and partner data in one tool. A farmer describes a field with eight signals, each tied to a real dataset: SMAP for soil moisture, GPM/IMERG for rainfall, Landsat and Sentinel-2 for plant health, NASA POWER for climate, SRTM for slope, ECOSTRESS and OpenET for water stress, Web Soil Survey for soil, and USDA data for market demand.
The advisor scores six crops (corn, soybeans, wheat, alfalfa, cotton, sorghum), applies rotation rules such as following non-legumes with legumes, and returns a ranked recommendation with plain-language reasons and a 3-year plan. A searchable catalog shows the role of all 25 challenge resources.
In demos, drought shifts advice to sorghum, a steep field favors alfalfa, and a field that just grew corn moves toward soybeans. The prototype uses simulated inputs and simplified scoring; next, signals will be filled automatically by location from NASA and USDA APIs.
details:
The challenge we addressed
Farmers know that rotating crops improves soil health, saves water and lowers risk from pests and weather. But deciding what to plant next means weighing soil moisture, rainfall, temperature, terrain, soil quality, crop history and market demand. This information sits in many separate portals, in different formats and scales. Most farmers, especially on small farms, don’t have the time or tools to combine it, so rotation choices often rely on habit instead of evidence.

Our solution
Field Shift is a web-based crop rotation advisor that turns NASA Earth observations and USDA and partner datasets into one clear decision: what to plant next. The user describes a field using eight signals (soil moisture, 30-day rainfall, vegetation health, temperature, slope, soil organic matter, water stress and local market demand) and the last crop grown. The advisor ranks six crops, explains the reasons behind the top choice, and proposes a 3-year rotation plan.

How the recommendation is made
Each crop has an ideal range for moisture, rainfall, temperature, slope and organic matter. The advisor measures how well the field matches those ranges, then adjusts the score in three ways. First, it penalizes water-hungry crops when evapotranspiration stress is high. Second, it applies rotation rules: it avoids repeating the last crop, and favors legumes after non-legumes to restore nitrogen. Third, it scales every score by local market demand, so the recommended crop is agronomically sound and also viable to sell.

How we use the data
We organized the 25 challenge resources into four roles. NASA satellites such as SMAP, GPM/IMERG, Landsat, MODIS/VIIRS, ECOSTRESS, SRTM and NASA POWER observe the field. Ground and reanalysis sources such as CoCoRaHS, USGS NWIS, OpenET, PRISM, ERA5 and NLDAS/GLDAS validate those observations and fill gaps. Soil and land-cover sources such as SSURGO, Web Soil Survey, the Cropland Data Layer, NLCD, LANDFIRE and FAO GAEZ give local context and crop history. USDA QuickStats and AMS Market News check yields and prices. A searchable data catalog in the app shows each dataset’s role and links to its source.

What the demo shows
In our demo scenarios, the recommendation changes as conditions change. When soil moisture and rainfall drop and water stress rises, drought-tolerant sorghum takes the top spot and corn falls sharply. When a field has a steep slope, alfalfa ranks first because its perennial cover tolerates erosion risk. When the last crop was corn on a balanced field, soybeans rank first because a legume restores nitrogen.

Impact
Field Shift makes satellite data usable by people who are not data scientists. It supports faster, evidence-based planting decisions, healthier soil, lower erosion risk and better water use during drought. The same approach could scale to other regions by swapping in local datasets.

Current status and next steps
The current version is a working prototype. Inputs are entered with sliders that stand in for real dataset values, and the scoring is a simplified model, not full agronomic advice. Our next steps are to fill the signals automatically by location using the NASA POWER, SMAP and IMERG APIs, let users draw their field boundary on a map, train a model on Cropland Data Layer history and QuickStats yields, and test the tool with local farmers and extension agents.
dataRefs: SMAP provides global measurements of surface soil moisture and freeze/thaw state, collected every 2–3 days. Soil‑moisture information helps identify drought stress, water availability, infiltration potential, and early crop‑stress signals. These data are valuable for evaluating rotation crops that could improve water efficiency, soil conditions, or drought resilience.
https://www.earthdata.nasa.gov/data/platforms/space-based-platforms/smap

The GPM mission and its IMERG product provide global precipitation rate and accumulation estimates. These help assess rainfall reliability, extreme‑storm frequency, erosion risk, water input to soils, and long‑term trends in field moisture. IMERG is valuable for comparing rotation strategies under different precipitation scenarios. (Worldview IMERG layers can be downloaded directly as high‑resolution images.)
https://gpm.nasa.gov/data

Agroclimatology & Meteorological Data: NASA POWER provides accessible solar, meteorological, and climatology datasets used widely in agriculture. The datasets include temperature, humidity, radiation, and derived indicators that help estimate crop water use, growing‑season conditions, frost risk, and climate suitability for potential rotation crops.
https://power.larc.nasa.gov/

Elevation & Terrain Models: The Shuttle Radar Topography Mission (SRTM) provides global elevation data suitable for analyzing slope, runoff, erosion risk, water flow, and terrain‑driven stress conditions. Terrain patterns help determine which rotation crops may improve infiltration, reduce erosion, or stabilize soil on slopes.
https://www.earthdata.nasa.gov/data/instruments/srtm

ECOSTRESS measures land‑surface temperature (LST) and evapotranspiration (ET) at high spatial resolution. This helps detect hotspots of plant stress, heat exposure, shallow‑root vulnerability, and crop‑water demand. It is particularly useful for identifying when current crops may be becoming more vulnerable and for mapping field‑level microclimate differences.
https://ecostress.jpl.nasa.gov/data

Open Access Agricultural Datasets: USDA’s Ag Data Commons provides open‑access agricultural datasets covering soils, crops, climate, land management, phenology, water quality, and ecological conditions. These datasets offer valuable ground‑based and agricultural context that can complement NASA’s satellite observations. Participants may use Ag Data Commons to incorporate local crop information, soil‑property measurements, management practices, and field‑level agricultural research into their models. These data can help SI tools align NASA’s environmental indicators with practical farm‑level constraints and crop‑rotation realities.
https://www.nal.usda.gov/services/agdatacommons

The WSS, maintained by USDA’s Natural Resources Conservation Service (NRCS), provides official U.S. soil data, including detailed soil maps, soil properties, drainage classifications, erosion risk, hydrologic ratings, and suitability for different land uses. Participants may use WSS to identify field‑specific soil characteristics—such as organic matter, texture, infiltration, and compaction risk—which can improve SI‑driven rotation recommendations. Integrating NASA Earth observations with WSS data may help teams build stronger, locally accurate interpretations of soil health and crop suitability.
https://websoilsurvey.nrcs.usda.gov/app/

The USDA CDL provides annual, high‑resolution (30‑meter) cropland classifications for the United States, identifying specific crop types such as corn, soybeans, cotton, wheat, alfalfa, and more. These data can help participants examine existing crop rotations, track changes across seasons, identify bare fields, evaluate crop suitability, and compare local cropping patterns with NASA‑observed environmental conditions. The CDL can also support SI models by supplying labeled land‑cover inputs tied to real agricultural production.
https://nassgeodata.gmu.edu/CropScape/

Oregon State University: PRISM provides high‑quality climate datasets for the United States, including daily, monthly, and 30‑year climate normals for precipitation, temperature, dewpoint, frost/freeze dates, and more. Because PRISM incorporates topographic effects, it offers highly accurate climate context for local farms. Participants may use PRISM to assess long‑term climate trends, align rotation strategies with local temperature and rainfall history, and validate environmental stress indicators derived from NASA satellites.
https://prism.oregonstate.edu/

Soil Data: SSURGO (field‑scale) and STATSGO2 (regional‑scale) provide detailed soil attributes such as texture, organic matter, drainage class, hydrologic soil group, erosion‑risk factors, restrictive layers, and water‑holding capacity. These data complement NASA observations by enabling accurate, location‑specific assessments of soil health, erosion potential, infiltration dynamics, and crop suitability. Integrating SSURGO with NASA datasets can help SI models produce more grounded and agronomically meaningful rotation suggestions.
https://www.nrcs.usda.gov/resources/data-and-reports/soils

NAIP provides high‑resolution (typically 1‑meter) aerial imagery captured during the U.S. growing season. These images allow participants to map field boundaries, detect bare soil periods, observe crop development, monitor land‑management changes, and assess vegetation cover at fine spatial scales. NAIP imagery can serve as a powerful input for training SI models that require closer‑than‑satellite detail or for validating crop and soil‑condition patterns detected from NASA Earth observations.
https://naip-usdaonline.hub.arcgis.com/

NLCD offers land‑cover and land‑use classifications at 30‑meter resolution across multiple decades. This dataset helps identify farmland, pasture, forested areas, water bodies, wetlands, and development zones near agricultural fields. Participants may use NLCD to contextualize landscape features that influence microclimates, water availability, erosion risk, and pest dynamics. NLCD also supports long‑term analysis of land‑cover change and its relationship to farm vulnerability.
https://www.usgs.gov/centers/eros/science/national-land-cover-database

NLDAS and GLDAS combine satellite and ground‑based meteorological observations to generate gridded datasets of temperature, precipitation, soil moisture, evapotranspiration proxies, radiation, and other surface variables at sub‑daily resolution. These datasets help participants study drought onset, moisture deficits, growing‑season transitions, and environmental stress conditions. When combined with NASA’s mission‑based datasets, NLDAS/GLDAS can enhance SI models by providing continuous time‑series climate features. (search “NLDAS” or “GLDAS” within Earthdata Search.)
https://www.earthdata.nasa.gov/

GAEZ provides global agro‑climatic suitability layers for dozens of crops, along with soil constraints, water availability indicators, yield potentials, and land‑productivity assessments. These resources can help participants evaluate whether proposed rotation crops align with local climate and soil conditions, and compare multiple rotation scenarios from a global agronomic perspective.
https://gaez.fao.org/

Community Rain/Snow Observations: CoCoRaHS offers crowd‑sourced daily precipitation measurements across North America. Participants may use this dataset to validate satellite rainfall estimates (such as IMERG), detect hyper‑local extreme rain events affecting specific fields, and refine model accuracy for water‑stress or irrigation‑timing predictions.
https://www.cocorahs.org/Maps

NWIS provides long‑term records of groundwater levels, streamflow, river stages, and water‑quality measurements. These data can help participants assess water availability for irrigation, identify hydrologic stress, understand downstream erosion risks, and compare NASA‑observed moisture conditions with in‑situ observations.
https://waterdata.usgs.gov/nwis

USDA Market News publishes commodity prices, demand trends, and market conditions for crops and livestock. Participants may use these data to help determine whether proposed rotation crops have viable markets locally or regionally—an important farmer‑driven constraint when evaluating rotation strategies.
https://www.ams.usda.gov/market-news

QuickStats provides county‑level and state‑level agricultural statistics, including yields, planted acreage, production history, and crop frequency. These data can help participants calibrate their models against historical performance, compare rotation possibilities, and explore long‑term agricultural trends.
https://quickstats.nass.usda.gov/

Evapotranspiration for Water Management: OpenET delivers field‑scale evapotranspiration estimates using satellite‑driven models for western U.S. states. Participants may use this dataset to evaluate crop water demand, irrigation timing, water‑use efficiency, and identify fields under thermal or moisture stress. OpenET offers valuable ground‑truth ET information that complements ECOSTRESS and NASA POWER.
https://openetdata.org/

Vegetation & Fuel Layers: LANDFIRE provides vegetation type, vegetation condition, fuel models, and landscape characteristics across the United States. These data may be used to understand local ecosystems, perennial cover, tree‑crop interactions, and landscape features that affect microclimates, water flow, erosion, and biodiversity relevant to rotational planning.
https://www.landfire.gov/

GEDI provides high‑resolution laser‑based measurements of forest structure, including canopy height, leaf area index, and above‑ground biomass. Participants may use GEDI Level‑4 biomass products to understand vegetation density, canopy stress, and long‑term ecosystem changes around agricultural landscapes. While GEDI is most effective in areas with taller vegetation, its biomass and canopy metrics can help identify shifts in surrounding land cover, detect environmental stress impacts, and complement rotation‑crop analysis by providing structural context that pairs well with SMAP, Landsat, and MODIS vegetation indicators.
https://gedi.umd.edu/data
projectRefs: Sentinel‑2 provides freely accessible 10–20‑meter multispectral imagery at high revisit frequency. With bands specifically designed for vegetation analysis (red‑edge, NIR, SWIR), participants may use Sentinel‑2 for NDVI/EVI, bare‑soil mapping, crop stress detection, and fine‑scale monitoring during growing seasons. Its higher spatial resolution complements Landsat and MODIS for field‑level assessments.

ERA5 is a global reanalysis dataset that provides hourly climate variables such as temperature, precipitation, wind, humidity, soil temperature, and radiation. Participants may use ERA5 to fill gaps where local weather stations are sparse, analyze long‑term climate trends, build temporal features for SI models, and contextualize NASA Earth observations with continuous climate time series.
